brief: A planter for a sunny kitchen windowsill with three herbs growing in it.
costSource: token-equivalent at Muse Spark Open shared rates, info only: the Dedicated Endpoint bills GPU seconds while up (.spend/modal-dedicated.jsonl)

requirements.requirement: Planter suitable for a sunny kitchen windowsill
requirements.evidence: Linear 3-cell planter (507 x 384 x 89mm parts, 163mm with plants) fits a typical windowsill depth/width. Built from 3x piece:full bases at q -1,0,0 / 0,0,0 / 1,0,0 with 3x hex-bin-full-drain bins (bin:-1,0,0~hex-bin-full-drain, bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-full-drain, bin:1,0,0~hex-bin-full-drain) — drained trays for watering on a sunny sill. Low linear form keeps sun exposure, ends capped with solid caps and joints bolted.

Each drained bin filled with soil and planted: basil-young in bin -1,0,0 (prop:1), parsley-young in bin 0,0,0 (prop:2), mint-young in bin 1,0,0 (prop:3) via fill_and_plant. Visible in look views (all 3 props seen from side and top). check_build OK, meshClash clear.

finish.summary: Built a compact linear planter of 3 connected hex cells (507mm long) with 3 drained full-depth bins, each filled with soil and planted with a different herb — basil, parsley and mint (young stage) — sized for a sunny kitchen windowsill. Caps and joint bolts applied, no collisions, all three plants visible.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
